paragraphs: A refinery reads as a refinery because of vertical scale against horizontal sprawl: distillation columns standing far above everything else, with drums, exchangers and pipe racks spread around their base. Take away the columns and the same site becomes a chemical works or a tank farm.

The mesh runs 1,747,442 polygons and 1,833,188 vertices in quads and tris. The UVs overlap, which is essential economy on a plant built from thousands of repeated flanges and fittings, and keeps a site this size workable.

At $229 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits oil and gas visualisation, energy sector marketing, infrastructure and environmental presentation, documentary and news work, film and television, and games. On sale since 2025.

A monster truck is a tube chassis with a fibreglass shell dropped over it and wheels taller than a person at each corner. The body is decorative rather than structural, which is why it can be any shape at all, and the suspension travel is what dictates the enormous gap between body and tyre.
The mesh runs 483,742 polygons and 494,125 vertices in quads and tris with mixed UV layout, with the density in the chassis tubes, the suspension links and the tyre tread.

This page carries a rigged build at $269 and a simplified version at $199. Aimed at motorsport and event visualisation, broadcast graphics, advertising, racing games and print. Built to CheckMate specification, on sale since 2026.

The two animals are confused constantly and are quite different: one has heavy front claws and short antennae, the other has no claws at all and antennae longer than its body. Supplying both in one collection is how a seafood or marine scene gets the distinction right rather than showing the same creature twice.
Both arrive rigged and prepared for Maya, which matters for crustaceans: the segmented tail and the multi jointed legs are tedious to rig and easy to get wrong.

A build prepared for Cinema 4D sits on this page at the same $229. Both suit seafood and restaurant visualisation, marine documentary and education, aquarium material, food advertising and games. On sale since 2020.

An offshore farm needs a boat, and adding one changes the whole story of the image: the pens become a workplace rather than floating equipment, with a vessel alongside for feeding, net inspection and harvest. That relationship is what an industry render is usually trying to show.
The mesh runs 622,895 polygons and 637,551 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, covering the cage array, the nets, the walkways and the support vessel.

At $229 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits aquaculture and seafood industry visualisation, food supply and sustainability presentation, marine and coastal scenes, documentary work and games. On sale since 2025.

A heavy lift ship submerges its own deck to float a cargo on, then pumps out and rises underneath it. That is why the deck is a bare flat expanse the length of the hull, with the accommodation and bridge pushed right forward and nothing at all in the way behind them.
The mesh runs 559,025 polygons and 587,703 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the density in the deck fittings, the buoyancy casings and the forward superstructure.

At $219 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits heavy marine transport visualisation, offshore energy and shipping presentation, port and salvage scenes, documentary work and games. On sale since 2025.

A modern battlefield radar is a flat panel on a trailer, tilted back and steered electronically rather than rotated. That single change removes the spinning dish everyone associates with radar and produces something that looks more like a billboard on a chassis than a sensor.
The mesh runs 123,548 polygons and 140,522 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the geometry in the array face, the mount and the trailer frame.

A rigged build sits on this page at $229 for when the array has to raise or rotate. The static model at $219 covers air defence and military visualisation, news and documentary graphics, procurement and training presentation, and games. On sale since 2021.

A maritime patrol aircraft is a turboprop airliner rebuilt to hunt submarines: a long fuselage full of sensor operators, a magnetic anomaly boom sticking out of the tail, and a weapons bay under the belly. That tail boom is the identification, and it is unlike anything on a civil aircraft.
The mesh is efficient at 143,915 polygons and 153,856 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and it arrives rigged so the propellers turn and the gear retracts.

This page carries a simplified build at $149 and rigged versions prepared for Cinema 4D and Maya at $219. Aimed at naval aviation and defence visualisation, documentary and news graphics, film and television, training material and games. On sale since 2025.

A loaded car transporter is one of the most complicated shapes on a road: two decks of ramps at different angles, vehicles nosed in at alternating heights, and hydraulics holding all of it. That geometric puzzle is the whole visual, and an empty transporter shows almost none of it.
It is a large asset at 2,094,481 polygons and 2,325,516 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and that weight is the cars: every vehicle on the deck is a complete model.

A Freightliner version sits on this page at $249. Both suit logistics and automotive transport visualisation, highway and dealership scenes, fleet marketing, film and television, and games. Built to CheckMate specification, on sale since 2025.

The passenger version of a large van is a different vehicle from the panel version: windows all the way down both sides, a raised roof line for headroom, and seating rather than a bulkhead behind the cab. It is the shuttle, minibus and airport transfer vehicle of most of the world.
The mesh runs 219,325 polygons and 245,125 vertices in quads and tris with mixed UV layout, and it arrives rigged so the wheels turn, the doors open and the sliding side door works.

At $219 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits transport and shuttle service visualisation, hospitality and airport scenes, fleet and commercial vehicle marketing, urban renders and games. On sale since 2026.

An articulated bus is two bodies joined by a turntable with a concertina over it, and that joint is the whole engineering problem: it has to carry passengers standing on it while the two halves pivot relative to each other. Modelled as a rigid long bus, the vehicle loses the feature that defines it.
The mesh runs 952,648 polygons and 979,247 vertices with mixed UV layout, and it arrives rigged so the wheels turn, the doors open and the articulation joint bends.

At $219 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits urban transit and city visualisation, public transport marketing, planning and infrastructure presentation, street scenes and games. On sale since 2026.

The building is shaped like a sail and stands on its own artificial island, which means it is almost always seen in isolation against sky and water. That isolation is unforgiving: there is no context to hide behind, and the curved membrane facade has to be exactly right from every angle.

The mesh runs 355,594 polygons and 411,350 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 30 texture maps including 8 at 8192x8192. Those large maps are the membrane, which needs to read as translucent fabric rather than as painted panel.
At $209 it suits architectural and city visualisation, hospitality and property marketing, travel and tourism material, film and television establishing shots, and games. On sale since 2020.

Defence analysis needs the order of battle rather than one vehicle: armour, artillery, air defence and support all at a consistent scale and finish, so a graphic can lay them out for comparison. Assembling that from separate purchases is where the mismatches show.
Supplying the platforms as one collection keeps the modelling standard consistent across the whole set, which matters most in exactly the wide comparative graphics these assets are bought for.

This page carries four other collections from $299 to $439, including rigged sets. This one at $209 suits defence and geopolitical visualisation, news and documentary graphics, strategic analysis material, training presentation and games. On sale since 2024.

This vessel exists to run rocket launches from the middle of the ocean: a mission control centre, a rocket assembly hall and a helideck on a converted hull. That combination is unique, and it explains the enormous flat superstructure block that dominates the ship.

The mesh runs 551,976 polygons and 642,799 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 13 texture maps all at 8192x8192 - an unusual choice that gives the hull plating and the deck markings real resolution over a long ship.

A rigged build sits on this page at $259. The static model at $209 covers space industry and maritime visualisation, documentary and news graphics, engineering presentation, museum material and games. On sale since 2018.

A period street needs a rank of taxis rather than one. Several cabs with variation between them - different wear, different roof lights, different positions - are what make a Manhattan scene read as a city rather than as a stage set, and every unit here arrives rigged so the wheels turn and the doors open.
Supplying them together also keeps the paint, the chrome and the ride height consistent between vehicles, which is what breaks when a fleet is assembled from separate purchases.
At $209 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits period film and television, urban and street visualisation, advertising, editorial imagery and games. On sale since 2020.
